answer:
No, you probably can't make the landlord fix this one, because your friend broke the window at your party. Windows are normally the landlord's job. But Florida's law says the landlord isn't responsible for damage caused by a guest you invited. Your lease also says you pay for damage caused by your guests. The office's answer matches both. The cold is a real problem, but the usual tools for forcing a repair (ending the lease or holding back rent) depend on the landlord's own repair duty. Those tools don't reach damage a guest caused.

Whether the landlord does the repair and bills you, or waits for you to pay first, is a different question. The statute doesn't answer it. Please don't hold back rent over this.

Has the office said it will do the repair and charge you, or that it won't touch the window until you pay?

DETAILS

### Are windows the landlord's job?
Usually, yes. Fla. Stat. 83.51(1)(b) says that where no building, housing, or health code applies, the landlord must keep the "windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair." Section 83.51(1)(a) also requires the landlord to comply with applicable building, housing, and health codes. I can't check those local codes here. The city or county code enforcement office can tell you whether one covers a broken window.

### Does it matter that your friend broke it?
Yes. Section 83.51(4) says the landlord "is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." You told me a friend you invited broke the window by accident. That makes your friend a person on the premises with your consent. So under 83.51 the window is not the landlord's duty to fix.

### What does your lease say?
Section 11 lists what the landlord keeps in working order: "refrigerator, stove, dishwasher, and central air conditioning." Windows are not on that list. Section 11 also says: "Tenant shall pay for repairing damage caused by Tenant, Tenant's household, or Tenant's guests." The lease therefore puts this repair on you.

### Can you end the lease or hold back rent?
Not on these facts. Ending the lease over a repair (83.56(1)) and the rent-withholding defense (83.60(1)(b)) both depend on the landlord failing a duty under 83.51(1) or the lease. Here, 83.51(4) and lease section 11 point the other way. If you withheld rent anyway, the landlord could file an eviction case. You would then have no defense based on this window.

### What if the landlord does the repair anyway?
Section 83.51(4) only says the landlord isn't responsible *under that section*. It doesn't say who pays if the landlord makes the repair. Lease section 11 answers that: you pay. The lease doesn't say how fast the landlord must act, or whether the landlord must act before you pay. That is why the office's reply to you matters.

Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Every option below starts here. Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a building, housing, or health code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored. The city or county code enforcement office can say, and can inspect the home.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Read every page of the lease for the item that broke: whether the lease lists it as provided (appliances, air conditioning, a washer and dryer, a pool or gym, parking, furniture, internet), who the lease says repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee paid for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - Air conditioning is not named in 83.51. It is the landlord's job if the lease says so, or if a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or "Purports to limit or preclude any liability of the landlord to the tenant or of the tenant to the landlord, arising under law." (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** "if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises (a pool, a dishwasher, air conditioning the lease lists), and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to "the landlord, the landlord's representative as designated pursuant to s. 83.50 , a resident manager, or the person or entity who collects the rent on behalf of the landlord" (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). The time is "5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process" (83.60(2)), and missing it "constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). This tool does not count those 5 days. Never give a date for them; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches an 83.51 duty and a lease promise alike, and 83.55 names no notice. Paying rent with knowledge matters here too: 83.56(5)(a) speaks of the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so give option 1's two readings on rent paid. How much, and how to bring the claim in court, is outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include "The tenant has complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises" (83.64(1)(a)) and "The tenant has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56 (1)" (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently is required: "a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in court: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

"If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered.
- Giving a date for the 83.60(2) registry deadline.
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and without 83.60(2).
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".

answer:
**Short answer:** You shouldn't stop paying rent over this, because Florida's rent-withholding defense doesn't cover air conditioning. You may be able to end the lease, but you haven't taken the required step yet. Your portal request doesn't count as the notice, so you can't leave yet without risk. Your lease promises working air conditioning, so ending the lease is available. You'd first have to hand-deliver or certified-mail a written notice to the office saying you will end the lease over the air conditioning. If the landlord hasn't fixed it within 7 days of that notice arriving, you may end the lease. You haven't paid rent since the air conditioning broke, which helps you.

Have you handed or mailed anything in writing to the office at Suite A, other than the portal request?

DETAILS

### Can you stop paying rent until it's fixed?
- The rent-withholding defense is in 83.60(1)(b). It covers only a "material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)". That subsection covers building, housing and health codes, structure, and plumbing.
- Air conditioning isn't named in 83.51. It's your landlord's job because your lease says so. Lease §11 says the landlord provides "central air conditioning" and "will keep them in working order."
- A lease-only duty doesn't support the rent-withholding defense. If you stopped paying, your landlord could file for eviction, and the air conditioning would not be a defense.
- A local building or housing code might require air conditioning. If it does, the answer could change. The tool doesn't store local codes. Gainesville or Alachua County code enforcement can tell you, and they can inspect.
- If you were ever sued, 83.60(2) requires you to pay the rent into the court registry within 5 days (not counting weekends and holidays) after you're served. The summons states this requirement. Missing it gives up your defenses other than payment.

### Can you end the lease?
Section 83.56(1) lets a tenant end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate." This applies because the air conditioning is a lease promise. Here is how your facts fit:
1. **A duty the landlord failed:** The lease promises working air conditioning (§11), and it has been out since June 3. The cause is nothing you know of, so 83.51(4) (damage you or your guests caused) doesn't appear to apply.
2. **Whether the failure is "material":** The statute doesn't define this, and it's not settled. One reading is that any failure of a lease promise counts. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there. Two weeks of 90-degree heat is the kind of fact the second reading would weigh.
3. **Proper written notice:** Not yet met. Your June 4 portal request asked for a repair. It didn't say you would end the lease. Section 83.56(4) names mailing or delivering a true copy as the ways to give notice. It also names e-mail, but only under a signed e-mail addendum (83.505(1)). Your lease says in §8 that you haven't agreed to e-mail notices, and a portal message isn't one of the named ways. Lease §7 says notices to the landlord go "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or by certified mail to that address. The notice should name the air conditioning problem and say you intend to end the lease because of it.
4. **Seven days:** The 7 days count from the day your notice reaches the office, not the day you send it. Hand delivery makes that date clear. Keep a copy.
5. **No rent paid with knowledge of the problem:** Met. You paid June rent on June 1, before the air conditioning stopped, and you've paid nothing since. Section 83.56(5)(a) says paying rent with knowledge of a problem can give up your right to end the lease over it. Whether that applies to a problem that is still going on is not settled. The July 1 payment could raise that issue. One reading is that an unfixed problem is a "continuing noncompliance," so paying gives up nothing. The other is that paying with knowledge gives up the right to end the lease over that failure. Keep this in mind before July 1.

### Does the "part on order" reply change this?
Section 83.56(1) has a separate rule for a failure caused by something "beyond the control of the landlord" when the landlord "has made and continues to make every reasonable effort." The outcome then is different:
- If the home is untenantable and you move out, you owe no rent while it stays that way.
- If you stay, the rent is reduced in proportion to the lost value.
- The statute says the lease may then be "terminated or altered by the parties." It's not settled whether that means both sides must agree or whether the rules apply on their own facts.
- "Untenantable" isn't defined. A part on order, with no update since June 4, may or may not show reasonable effort. Whether the landlord is still making effort would matter here.

### Can you recover money?
Section 83.55 lets you recover damages caused by the landlord's failure to meet the lease. It names no notice requirement. How much you could recover, and how to bring a claim, is outside this tool.

### Are you protected if the landlord retaliates?
Section 83.64(1) bars a landlord from raising rent, cutting services, or suing primarily to retaliate against a tenant who complains in good faith to a code office or gives notice under 83.56(1). It's a defense in an eviction case (83.64(2)). It doesn't apply if the landlord has good cause, and unpaid rent counts as good cause (83.64(3)).

Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Every option below starts here. Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a building, housing, or health code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored. The city or county code enforcement office can say, and can inspect the home.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Read every page of the lease for the item that broke: whether the lease lists it as provided (appliances, air conditioning, a washer and dryer, a pool or gym, parking, furniture, internet), who the lease says repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee paid for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - Air conditioning is not named in 83.51. It is the landlord's job if the lease says so, or if a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or "Purports to limit or preclude any liability of the landlord to the tenant or of the tenant to the landlord, arising under law." (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** "if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises (a pool, a dishwasher, air conditioning the lease lists), and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to "the landlord, the landlord's representative as designated pursuant to s. 83.50 , a resident manager, or the person or entity who collects the rent on behalf of the landlord" (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). The time is "5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process" (83.60(2)), and missing it "constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). This tool does not count those 5 days. Never give a date for them; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches an 83.51 duty and a lease promise alike, and 83.55 names no notice. Paying rent with knowledge matters here too: 83.56(5)(a) speaks of the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so give option 1's two readings on rent paid. How much, and how to bring the claim in court, is outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include "The tenant has complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises" (83.64(1)(a)) and "The tenant has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56 (1)" (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently is required: "a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in court: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

"If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered.
- Giving a date for the 83.60(2) registry deadline.
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and without 83.60(2).
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".

answer:
No. Florida's rent-withholding rule doesn't cover a broken dishwasher or a closed pool, so holding back part of your rent would not give you legal protection. The rule only covers a short list of the landlord's repair duties, such as the building's structure and plumbing. Your lease promises the dishwasher and the pool, but the withholding rule doesn't reach lease promises. If you short the rent, your landlord could file for eviction, and you would have no withholding defense to raise.

You still have other options. You can send a written notice that you will end the lease, and you can sue for damages. Both can work for items the lease promises. Both are affected by the fact that you paid May rent on May 1, after the problems began.

Your portal requests are not enough for a notice to end the lease. They ask for repairs but don't say you will leave, and the law doesn't list the portal as a way to deliver that notice. Handing the notice to the office or mailing it does meet the law.

Have you handed or mailed anything on paper to the office at Suite A, or has everything gone through the portal?

DETAILS

### Does the rent-withholding rule reach a dishwasher or a pool?
- The rule is § 83.60(1)(b). It allows the defense only for "a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)."
- Section 83.51(1) covers building, housing and health codes. Where no code applies, it covers structural parts and the plumbing.
- A dishwasher and a pool are not structure or plumbing.
- Whether a local code covers either one is outside this tool. The city or county code enforcement office can tell you.
- Your lease is where these two items come from. Lease § 11 says the landlord "will keep them in working order," and it lists the dishwasher. It also says residents "may use the community pool from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m."
- These are lease promises, not § 83.51(1) duties. So withholding under § 83.60(1)(b) is not available for them.

### What happens if you hold back rent anyway?
- Your landlord could file an eviction case for unpaid rent.
- If sued, you would have to pay the rent into the court registry within 5 days (not counting weekends and holidays) after you are served (§ 83.60(2)). The summons will state this. Missing it "constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment."
- Since the rent-withholding defense doesn't reach these items, paying into the registry would not protect you here.

### Can you end the lease over these problems?
- The rule is § 83.56(1). If the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement" within 7 days after you deliver a written notice, you "may terminate the rental agreement." The notice must name the problem and say you intend to end the lease because of it.
- The dishwasher is named in lease § 11, so it is a lease promise. The pool is more doubtful. The lease lets the landlord "close the pool for cleaning, repairs, or weather." It says nothing about a closure with no end date.
- Whether a failure is "material" is not settled. One reading is that any failure to keep a lease promise counts. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects your life there. A dishwasher out for about three weeks and a pool closed for about a month fit both readings.
- On the pool clause, there are two readings. One is that the clause only describes what the lease promises, so a closure the landlord is allowed to make is not a failure. The other is that the clause is void under § 83.47(1) to the extent it takes away rights Florida's law gives you. Neither reading is settled.
- Delivery matters. Under § 83.56(4), the notice must be mailed or handed over, or e-mailed under § 83.505. Lease § 8 says there is no e-mail agreement. Lease § 7 says to hand it to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it there by certified mail. The portal is not a way § 83.56(4) names. Lease § 11 asks for repair requests through the portal. It cannot take away the notice rules, because "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement" (§ 83.56(4)).
- Paying rent can give up this right. Under § 83.56(5)(a), if you pay rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance," you give up the right to end the lease over it, "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." You paid on May 1 knowing about both problems. One reading is that problems still unfixed are a "continuing noncompliance," so your payment gave up nothing. The other is that paying with knowledge gave up the right as to these failures. This is not settled.

### Can you recover money?
- Under § 83.55, if the landlord fails to comply with the lease or this law, you "may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." It names no notice requirement.
- Section 83.56(5)(a) also mentions the right "to bring a civil action." So the same two readings on your May 1 payment apply here.
- How much you could recover, and how to bring the claim, is outside this tool.

### Does the cause matter?
- You said nothing you did caused the problems. Under § 83.51(4), the landlord is not responsible only for what you, your family or your guests cause. That doesn't apply here.

Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Every option below starts here. Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a building, housing, or health code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored. The city or county code enforcement office can say, and can inspect the home.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Read every page of the lease for the item that broke: whether the lease lists it as provided (appliances, air conditioning, a washer and dryer, a pool or gym, parking, furniture, internet), who the lease says repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee paid for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - Air conditioning is not named in 83.51. It is the landlord's job if the lease says so, or if a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or "Purports to limit or preclude any liability of the landlord to the tenant or of the tenant to the landlord, arising under law." (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** "if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises (a pool, a dishwasher, air conditioning the lease lists), and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to "the landlord, the landlord's representative as designated pursuant to s. 83.50 , a resident manager, or the person or entity who collects the rent on behalf of the landlord" (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). The time is "5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process" (83.60(2)), and missing it "constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). This tool does not count those 5 days. Never give a date for them; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches an 83.51 duty and a lease promise alike, and 83.55 names no notice. Paying rent with knowledge matters here too: 83.56(5)(a) speaks of the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so give option 1's two readings on rent paid. How much, and how to bring the claim in court, is outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include "The tenant has complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises" (83.64(1)(a)) and "The tenant has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56 (1)" (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently is required: "a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in court: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

"If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered.
- Giving a date for the 83.60(2) registry deadline.
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and without 83.60(2).
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".

answer:
Probably not, if your landlord raised the rent mainly to punish you for the mold complaint. A rent increase is not illegal just because it is large. But Florida law bans a rent increase that treats one tenant differently, and that is done mainly as payback for a complaint to a code office. Your facts fit that pattern: you complained, the inspector came, and three days later only your rent went up. Whether the law was actually broken depends on your landlord's main reason, and a court would decide that.

The law is not a flat rule against retaliation. If your landlord says the increase has a different reason, such as market rates, a court would have to weigh that against the timing. If you stop paying the higher rent, the retaliation point works as a defense if your landlord sues to evict you. It is not a way to avoid the increase before that happens. So don't withhold any rent without getting advice first.

What reason, if any, did your landlord give for the increase, in the letter or in person?

DETAILS

### Does Florida law ban this kind of rent increase?
Under s. 83.64(1), it is unlawful for a landlord "to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent" "primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." The same subsection lists examples of protected conduct. One example, in (1)(a), is when the tenant "has complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises." Your April 28 complaint to city code enforcement is that kind of complaint.

### Do your facts show different treatment?
Section 83.64(4) says "discrimination" means a tenant "is being treated differently as to the rent charged." That difference is required before retaliation can be found. Two neighbors told you their rent did not change, while yours went from $1,050 to $1,300. That is the kind of difference the law looks for. One caution: what the neighbors told you is not something I can check. Their rent may also change later.

### What does your landlord have to be thinking for this to count?
The law requires that the landlord acted "primarily because" of the retaliation. The timing helps you: the inspector came May 5, and the letter is dated May 8. But timing alone does not settle your landlord's reason.
- **Your side:** The complaint, the three-day gap, and the neighbors paying the old rent all point to payback.
- **Landlord's side:** They can say the increase was planned anyway, or based on market rent, or that other tenants will get increases too.

### Do you have to have acted in good faith?
Yes. Section 83.64(1) says the tenant "must have acted in good faith." You told me the mold started in March and that you did not cause it. That supports good faith. I have no sign your complaint was anything but real.

### What does the lease say?
Clause 3 makes the tenancy month to month. Clause 4 sets rent at $1,050 and says nothing about increases. Clause 10 says the lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." You could argue that clause means the increase has no effect unless you sign. Your landlord could answer that a month-to-month tenancy can be ended on notice, so new terms can be set that way. I did not find a statute in this part that settles that point, so I can't say which reading wins.

### What about being told to leave or being sued?
Section 83.64(1) also bars bringing or threatening an eviction "primarily because the landlord is retaliating." Under s. 83.64(2), you may raise retaliation as a defense in an eviction case. Under s. 83.64(3), the defense does not apply if the landlord proves the eviction is for "good cause," such as a good faith action for nonpayment of rent. A landlord can also end a month-to-month tenancy with at least 30 days' written notice before the end of a monthly period (s. 83.57(3)). Whether retaliation would defeat such a notice is a question I'd treat as open. No eviction has been filed.

### What can't I tell from the statute?
The text I read gives retaliation as a defense in an eviction case. It does not say whether you can sue on your own for the increase. Local code enforcement or a legal aid office could tell you more about that.

answer:
It's not settled whether you can end your lease now, and I can't say yes or no. Your letter and the 7-day wait look fine. Two points are open: whether the law counts a broken water heater as something the landlord must fix, and whether paying March rent hurts you. If you move out and a court later disagrees, the landlord could say you still owe rent. Your lease says nothing about hot water or repairs, so it doesn't help either way.

Is there a city or county code enforcement office you've complained to, or a written code that covers hot water in your building? That could decide the first open point.

DETAILS

### Was your notice valid, and did the 7 days pass?
Yes on both, as far as the facts you confirmed show.
- Section 83.56(1) requires written notice that names the problem and says you intend to end the lease because of it. Your letter said the water heater is broken and that you will end the lease if it isn't fixed in 7 days.
- Section 83.56(4) allows delivery by "mailing" the notice. Lease §7 also allows certified mail to the office. The office signed for your letter on 2026-03-09.
- The 7 days ran to 2026-03-16, and that date has passed. The landlord has not fixed the heater.

### Does the landlord's duty cover hot water?
This is not settled. Your home is a unit in a larger building, so section 83.51(2)(a)5 applies. It requires "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water."

Ending the lease under section 83.56(1) reaches only a failure of section 83.51(1) or of a "material provision" of the lease. There are two readings:
- **Reading one:** A broken water heater is a plumbing problem. Section 83.51(1)(b) requires "the plumbing in reasonable working condition." Section 83.51(3) says that if the subsection (1) duty is "the same or greater" than the subsection (2) duty, subsection (1) controls. Under this reading, you can end the lease.
- **Reading two:** Hot water is named in subsection (2), so it is a subsection (2) duty. Section 83.56(1) mentions only subsection (1) and the lease. Under this reading, you can't end the lease on this ground, unless a building, housing, or health code also requires hot water (section 83.51(1)(a)).

The codes aren't stored in this tool. Your city or county code enforcement office can tell you whether a code covers hot water. The lease has no clause on hot water, appliances, or repairs. It doesn't supply a duty of its own.

### Is the failure "material"?
This is also not settled, because the statute doesn't define the word. There are two readings:
- **Reading one:** Any failure of a listed duty is material.
- **Reading two:** It depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there. You've had no hot water since 2026-02-25, and the landlord hasn't responded to your letter. Those facts help you under this reading.

### Does paying March rent hurt you?
This is not settled. You paid March rent on 2026-03-01, after the problem began on 2026-02-25. Section 83.56(5)(a) says a tenant who pays rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" gives up the right to end the lease "for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." There are two readings:
- **Reading one:** A heater that is still broken is a "continuing noncompliance," so paying rent gave up nothing.
- **Reading two:** You paid knowing about the problem, so you gave up the right to end the lease over this failure. Only a new failure would start the process over.

### Can you simply stop paying rent and stay?
That is a different route, and it is riskier. Section 83.60(1)(b) lets a tenant use a landlord's failure as a defense to an eviction for unpaid rent. It applies only to a section 83.51(1) duty. It also requires a written notice saying you will not pay rent because of the problem. Your letter said only that you would end the lease, so it wouldn't serve as that notice. Section 83.51(2)(c) says a subsection (2) duty can't be raised as a defense to an eviction. If the landlord sues, you must pay the rent into the court registry within the time stated in the summons (section 83.60(2)). If you miss that deadline, you lose your defenses.

### What happens if you do move out?
Under section 83.56(6), the landlord must follow section 83.49(3), which covers your $1,050 deposit. Lease §6 asks for a written forwarding address and the return of your keys. Lease §8 says notices after move-out go to the forwarding address you give in writing.

Every option below starts here. Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
