Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Every option below starts here. Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a building, housing, or health code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored. The city or county code enforcement office can say, and can inspect the home.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Read every page of the lease for the item that broke: whether the lease lists it as provided (appliances, air conditioning, a washer and dryer, a pool or gym, parking, furniture, internet), who the lease says repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee paid for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - Air conditioning is not named in 83.51. It is the landlord's job if the lease says so, or if a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or "Purports to limit or preclude any liability of the landlord to the tenant or of the tenant to the landlord, arising under law." (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** "if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises (a pool, a dishwasher, air conditioning the lease lists), and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to "the landlord, the landlord's representative as designated pursuant to s. 83.50 , a resident manager, or the person or entity who collects the rent on behalf of the landlord" (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). The time is "5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process" (83.60(2)), and missing it "constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). This tool does not count those 5 days. Never give a date for them; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches an 83.51 duty and a lease promise alike, and 83.55 names no notice. Paying rent with knowledge matters here too: 83.56(5)(a) speaks of the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so give option 1's two readings on rent paid. How much, and how to bring the claim in court, is outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include "The tenant has complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises" (83.64(1)(a)) and "The tenant has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56 (1)" (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently is required: "a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in court: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

"If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered.
- Giving a date for the 83.60(2) registry deadline.
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and without 83.60(2).
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".

### Did your letter meet the notice rules?
- **Delivery:** Yes. The statute allows notice "by mailing" (83.56(4)). Your certified letter reached the office on 2026-03-09.
- **Lease clause 7:** It asks for notices to go by hand or certified mail to the office. You did that. The statute also says these notice rules "may not be waived in the rental agreement" (83.56(4)).
- **Content:** Your letter named the broken water heater and said you would end the lease if it wasn't fixed in 7 days. That is what 83.56(1) asks for.
- **Seven days:** Counted from the day it was delivered, the 7 days ended 2026-03-16. That date has passed, and you report no repair.

### Is a broken water heater the kind of failure that lets you end the lease?
Section 83.56(1) lets you end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement." There are two open questions here.
- **Which part of the law covers hot water?** Your lease doesn't mention hot water or repairs, so the statute decides this.
  - **Reading one:** A water heater is part of the plumbing. Section 83.51(1)(b) requires "the plumbing in reasonable working condition." Under that reading, 83.56(1) applies directly.
  - **Reading two:** Section 83.51(2)(a)5 names "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water" for buildings like yours. Section 83.51(3) says that if the subsection (1) duty is "the same or greater," subsection (1) controls. Some would say hot water is only a subsection (2) duty. Subsection (2) is not covered by 83.56(1) unless a building, housing, or health code also requires hot water. I can't check local codes. The Gainesville or Alachua County code enforcement office can tell you.
- **Is it "material"?** The statute doesn't define the word.
  - **Reading one:** Any failure of a listed duty is material.
  - **Reading two:** It depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there. Here, there has been no hot water since 2026-02-25, and the landlord has not answered.

### Did paying March rent cost you the right to end the lease?
- You paid March rent on 2026-03-01, after you noticed the problem on 2026-02-25. Section 83.56(5)(a) says a tenant who "pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" gives up the right to end the lease over that noncompliance, "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance."
- **Reading one:** A heater that is still broken is a "continuing noncompliance," so the March payment gave up nothing.
- **Reading two:** Paying with knowledge gave up the right to end the lease over this failure, and only a new failure would start it over.

### Can you stop paying rent?
- Holding back rent is a separate route under 83.60(1)(b). It needs a written notice saying you will not pay rent because of the problem, and then 7 days must pass. Your letter did not say that.
- That route only covers failures of 83.51(1). Whether hot water falls under it is the same open question as above. Section 83.51(2)(c) says a subsection (2) failure can't be used as a defense to an eviction for possession.
- The risk is that your landlord can file an eviction case. If you are sued, you must pay the rent into the court registry within 5 days (not counting weekends and legal holidays) after you are served (83.60(2)). Missing that deadline waives your defenses other than payment. The summons will state the requirement.

### What if you do move out?
Section 83.56(6) says that once a rental agreement is terminated, the landlord must follow the security deposit rules in 83.49(3). Your lease (clause 6) also asks you to leave the unit clean and empty, return the keys, and give a forwarding address in writing.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Every option below starts here. Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a building, housing, or health code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored. The city or county code enforcement office can say, and can inspect the home.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Read every page of the lease for the item that broke: whether the lease lists it as provided (appliances, air conditioning, a washer and dryer, a pool or gym, parking, furniture, internet), who the lease says repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee paid for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - Air conditioning is not named in 83.51. It is the landlord's job if the lease says so, or if a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or "Purports to limit or preclude any liability of the landlord to the tenant or of the tenant to the landlord, arising under law." (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** "if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises (a pool, a dishwasher, air conditioning the lease lists), and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to "the landlord, the landlord's representative as designated pursuant to s. 83.50 , a resident manager, or the person or entity who collects the rent on behalf of the landlord" (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). The time is "5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process" (83.60(2)), and missing it "constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). This tool does not count those 5 days. Never give a date for them; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches an 83.51 duty and a lease promise alike, and 83.55 names no notice. Paying rent with knowledge matters here too: 83.56(5)(a) speaks of the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so give option 1's two readings on rent paid. How much, and how to bring the claim in court, is outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include "The tenant has complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises" (83.64(1)(a)) and "The tenant has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56 (1)" (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently is required: "a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in court: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

"If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered.
- Giving a date for the 83.60(2) registry deadline.
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and without 83.60(2).
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".

tool_calls.result: 83.51 Landlord’s obligation to maintain premises. — (1) The landlord at all times during the tenancy shall: (a) Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes; or (b) Where there are no applicable building, housing, or health codes, maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition. The landlord, at commencement of the tenancy, must ensure that screens are installed in a reasonable condition. Thereafter, the landlord must repair damage to screens once annually, when necessary, until termination of the rental agreement. The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant. The landlord’s obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex. (2)(a) Unless otherwise agreed in writing, in addition to the requirements of subsection (1), the landlord of a dwelling unit other than a single-family home or duplex shall, at all times during the tenancy, make reasonable provisions for: 1. The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs. If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent. The landlord must provide 7 days’ written notice, in person, by mail, or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 , to the tenant if the tenant must temporarily vacate the premises for extermination pursuant to this subparagraph. A tenant is only required to vacate the premises for a period of time not to exceed 4 days. 2. Locks and keys. 3. The clean and safe condition of common areas. 4. Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor. 5. Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water. (b) Unless otherwise agreed in writing, at the commencement of the tenancy of a single-family home or duplex, the landlord shall install working smoke detection devices. As used in this paragraph, the term “smoke detection device” means an electrical or battery-operated device which detects visible or invisible particles of combustion and which is listed by Underwriters Laboratories, Inc., Factory Mutual Laboratories, Inc., or any other nationally recognized testing laboratory using nationally accepted testing standards. (c) Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59 . (d) This subsection shall not apply to a mobile home owned by a tenant. (e) Nothing contained in this subsection prohibits the landlord from providing in the rental agreement that the tenant is obligated to pay costs or charges for garbage removal, water, fuel, or utilities. (3) If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord’s duty is determined by subsection (1). (4) The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant’s family, or other person on the premises with the tenant’s consent. History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 22, ch. 82-66; s. 4, ch. 87-195; s. 1, ch. 90-133; s. 3, ch. 93-255; s. 444, ch. 95-147; s. 8, ch. 97-95; s. 6, ch. 2013-136; s. 4, ch. 2025-16.

tool_calls.name: get_statute_section
tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due. answer:
**Short answer:** Not yet. If you skip May rent now, you risk an eviction case, and you probably couldn't use the leak as a defense. Florida law lets you use a bad roof as a defense to an eviction for unpaid rent. To do that, you must first give your landlord a written notice that names the problem and says you won't pay rent because of it. Then 7 days must pass. So far you've only phoned, and phone calls don't count. Even with the notice, a court would still decide two things. One is whether the leak is serious enough to count. The other is how much your rent would be reduced.

DETAILS

### Does Florida's landlord-tenant law cover your home?
Yes, as far as I can tell. Your lease is an ordinary apartment lease with Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC. Nothing in it ties your home to a school, medical care, or any of the other exclusions in 83.42. I've noted that as a pending fact for you to confirm.

### Is the roof your landlord's job to fix?
Yes. Under 83.51(1)(b), where no local code applies, the landlord must "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair." A local building or housing code may also cover this (83.51(1)(a)). I can't check local codes. Your city or county code enforcement office can tell you.

You say rain caused the leak and you did nothing to cause it. The landlord is not responsible only for problems the tenant, the tenant's family, or the tenant's guests cause (83.51(4)). So that exception doesn't apply here. You live in a unit in a larger building, so the landlord can't change this duty through the lease. Your lease also says nothing about repairs that would change it.

### What must you do before holding back rent?
Under 83.60(1)(b), you can raise the roof problem as a defense only "if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof."

- **What it must say:** It must name the leak and say you will not pay rent because of it. A letter that only asks for a repair doesn't meet this.
- **Who can receive it:** The landlord, a designated representative, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent (83.60(1)(b)).
- **How to deliver it:** The statute names no method for this notice, so that point is not settled. One reading is that any written notice reaching the right person counts, including e-mail or a portal message. The other reading is that part II's delivery rules apply (83.56(4)). On that reading, e-mail counts only with a signed e-mail addendum. Your lease says the parties "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail" (§8), and a portal message or text would not count. Handing the notice over or mailing it works under both readings. Your lease (§7) says to hand-deliver to 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it by certified mail. Doing it that way is safest.
- **Timing:** The 7 days start on the day the notice reaches the landlord, not the day you send it. I can't give a date until you have a delivery date.

Without this notice, holding back May 1 rent would leave you with no roof defense if the landlord sues for nonpayment.

### Is the leak serious enough?
This is not settled. The statute doesn't define "material." One reading is that any failure to maintain the roof is material. The other is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there. Your facts are a leak into the bedroom every time it rains, for about a month, with two unanswered calls.

### What happens if the landlord sues?
Holding back rent risks an eviction case even if you have a defense. If you are sued, 83.60(2) requires you to pay the rent into the court registry. That means the rent claimed in the complaint plus rent that comes due while the case is pending. You have 5 days, not counting weekends and legal holidays, after you are served. Missing that deadline is "an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment," and the landlord can get an immediate judgment for possession. The summons will state the requirement. If you win on the roof, the court decides how much, if any, your rent is reduced (83.60(1)(b)).

### Are there other options?
- **Ending the lease (83.56(1)):** You would send a written notice that names the problem and says you will end the lease. If the landlord doesn't fix it within 7 days after delivery, you may end the lease. You paid April rent on April 1, after you knew about the leak. Whether that gave up this right is not settled. One reading is that an unfixed roof is a "continuing noncompliance," so paying rent gives up nothing. The other is that paying with knowledge gives up the right for that failure (83.56(5)(a)).
- **Damages (83.55):** You can recover damages the leak caused you.
- **Code complaint:** Landlords may not retaliate against a tenant who complains in good faith to a code office (83.64(1)(a)).

Has your landlord or manager said anything about when the roof will be fixed, or why it hasn't been?

tool_calls.result:
Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Every option below starts here. Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a building, housing, or health code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored. The city or county code enforcement office can say, and can inspect the home.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Read every page of the lease for the item that broke: whether the lease lists it as provided (appliances, air conditioning, a washer and dryer, a pool or gym, parking, furniture, internet), who the lease says repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee paid for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - Air conditioning is not named in 83.51. It is the landlord's job if the lease says so, or if a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or "Purports to limit or preclude any liability of the landlord to the tenant or of the tenant to the landlord, arising under law." (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** "if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises (a pool, a dishwasher, air conditioning the lease lists), and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to "the landlord, the landlord's representative as designated pursuant to s. 83.50 , a resident manager, or the person or entity who collects the rent on behalf of the landlord" (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). The time is "5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process" (83.60(2)), and missing it "constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). This tool does not count those 5 days. Never give a date for them; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches an 83.51 duty and a lease promise alike, and 83.55 names no notice. Paying rent with knowledge matters here too: 83.56(5)(a) speaks of the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so give option 1's two readings on rent paid. How much, and how to bring the claim in court, is outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include "The tenant has complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises" (83.64(1)(a)) and "The tenant has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56 (1)" (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently is required: "a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in court: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

"If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered.
- Giving a date for the 83.60(2) registry deadline.
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and without 83.60(2).
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
